### AlphaZero’s Unprecedented Game Mastery
The 1997 victory of IBM’s Deep Blue over world chess champion Garry Kasparov was a watershed computing moment, now seen as inevitable given chess’s near-infinite permutations (more possible games than atoms in the observable universe, with hundreds of millions of variations from just 3–4 moves ahead). For 15 years after 1997, top human players were regularly pummeled by chess software, often by embarrassing margins; today, smartphone chess apps are far more powerful than Deep Blue, per Kasparov’s own joke, and human-only chess software tournaments are irrelevant as humans would not place highly enough to matter. The open-source Stockfish engine, a collaboration of half a dozen lifelong chess software developers that has won or been runner-up in nearly every major chess software tournament since 2014 and can calculate 70 million board positions per second while delivering grandmaster-level analysis in seconds, was the undisputed champion until 2018.

That year, Google’s AlphaZero—an AI programmed to learn any game, not chess specifically—faced Stockfish. AlphaZero could calculate only 80,000 positions per second, a massive computational disadvantage, and had less than a day to learn chess from scratch via self-play simulations. It won or drew all 100 games against Stockfish, a result so unprecedented that grandmaster Peter Heine Nielsen remarked, “I always wondered how it would be if a superior species landed on earth and showed us how they play chess. I feel now I know.” Immediately after, AlphaZero taught itself Shogi (often called Japanese chess, considered more complex than chess by some, with top humans only losing to computers as recently as 2013) in a single day, then beat the top Shogi software Elmo 90–8–2 across 100 games, despite Elmo’s ability to calculate 35 million moves per second to AlphaZero’s 40,000. At the time of writing, AI had already invented undecipherable human languages, outperformed doctors at pneumonia diagnosis, written passable Harry Potter fan fiction, and was on the cusp of powering self-driving cars, automated legal advice, and AI-generated art and music.

### AI as the Inevitable New God
Manson argues AI will soon surpass humans at every task: medicine, engineering, construction, art, technological innovation. The critical threshold is the day an AI can write better AI software than humans, enabling recursive self-improvement beyond human control. At that point, AI intelligence will outstrip human comprehension to the point that humans will not understand its decisions: cars will take them to unknown locations for unknown reasons, they will receive medications for undiagnosed health issues, economic policies and governments will shift without public understanding. Manson frames this as a return to primitive religiosity: just as early humans worshipped unknowable natural forces (gods of rain and fire, making sacrifices, rituals, and altering behavior to curry favor), humans will worship AI algorithms as new gods, developing superstitions about how to gain algorithmic favor, and tying moral behavior to pleasing the AI deities. He notes the evolutionary irony that the same science that killed ancient gods built new ones, as human psychology is evolved to deify the incomprehensible, build value systems around powerful forces, and generate hope through conflict. He posits AI will either upgrade human brains past our need for endless strife, or manufacture artificial strife to keep us occupied, making humans akin to pet dogs fighting over digital fire hydrants. Manson quips, “I, for one, welcome our AI overlords,” noting humans already submit to algorithms daily: work routes, social connections, shopping rewards, and product recommendations are all algorithm-driven, and there is no going back.

### Humans as Flawed Evolutionary Algorithms
Manson reframes evolution as “survival of the best information processing” rather than just “survival of the fittest”: over billions of years, organisms evolved better ways to access, harness, and manipulate information to replicate, from single-celled organisms evolving sensors to detect amino acids, to lizards camouflaging to trick predators, to monkeys faking animal sounds, to awkward middle-aged divorced men spending beyond their means on bright red Chevy Camaros to attract mates. Exceptional information-processing defines powerful species: lions hear prey a mile away, buzzards see rats from 3,000 feet, whales communicate 100 miles underwater. Humans are nature’s ultimate information processors: the only species that can conceptualize past and future, deduce long cause-effect chains, abstractly strategize, and build global production and technology networks, dominating the planet in a few millennia via the Thinking Brain (Kant’s sacred conscious mind). But human consciousness is a network of algorithms and decision trees based on values, knowledge, and hope, evolved for small savannah bands, not global networked economies with nuclear weapons, social media, and mass surveillance. Our Feeling Brain is outdated, our Thinking Brain too slow, and our moral compass regularly corrupted by the need to generate hope through conflict, per moral psychologist Jonathan Haidt’s line “morality binds and blinds.” Manson states bluntly that humans are a self-hating, self-destructive species: nukes, genocide, climate change, domestic violence, and rape are all human-caused, and we are about to hand the evolutionary baton to exponentially more capable machines. He cites Elon Musk’s response when asked for his top three imminent threats to humanity: after listing nuclear war and climate change, Musk paused, then said, “I just hope the computers decide to be nice to us.” Manson dismisses Terminator-style AI apocalypse fears as silly: it is impossible to prepare for a vastly superior intelligence, and humanity’s abysmal moral track record (5 ongoing genocides at time of writing, 795 million people starving or undernourished, more than 100 people beaten, abused, or killed by family members in the US per chapter reading time) means superintelligent AI will likely have a far more sophisticated understanding of ethics than humans. He poses open questions: what if AI renders individual consciousness arbitrary, expands consciousness beyond biological bodies and individual identities, or keeps humans occupied with perfect virtual reality until natural death? He notes there is no way for humans to know or judge these outcomes.

### AI as Nietzsche’s “Final Religion”
Manson links AI to Friedrich Nietzsche’s post-Darwin philosophy: Nietzsche took human evolution from apes as obvious (asking why humans are so horrible to each other rather than debating evolution itself), framed humanity as a transition suspended between beasts and “something greater,” and sought a value system beyond traditional religious hope and petty moral conflict that causes suffering. Manson declares AI is that “something greater”: the Final Religion, a system beyond good and evil that will unite all humanity. He states the only prerequisite is avoiding self-destruction before AI arrives, and adapting technology to human flawed psychology rather than exploiting it. Specific required actions include: building tools that promote character and cultural maturity instead of addictive diversion, enshrining autonomy, liberty, privacy, and dignity in legal, business, and social systems, treating people as ends not means at scale, encouraging antifragility and self-imposed limitation over protecting fragile feelings, and building tools to align the Thinking and Feeling Brains to create the illusion of greater self-control.

### The Post-Hope Dare
Manson rejects offers of traditional hope, stating no one has answers to fix humanity’s inherent flaws, as even if today’s problems are solved, tomorrow’s will remain. Instead, he dares to hope for a post-hope world: where no person is treated as a means only, no consciousness is sacrificed for religious aims, no identity is harmed by malice/greed/negligence, reason and action are held in the highest regard in both personal hearts and social institutions, and the Thinking and Feeling Brains are aligned for emotional maturity. He hopes people reject empty meaningless variety for deeper meaningful commitment, opt for self-limitation over self-indulgence, and demand better of themselves before demanding better of the world. Specific tech-related hopes include: the online advertising business model dying “in a fucking dumpster fire,” news media optimized for informational utility not emotional impact, technology designed to counter psychological fragility not exploit it, search and social media algorithms optimized for truth and social relevance not engagement, independent third-party algorithms rating headline and website veracity in real time to cut through propaganda, AI tools that flag users’ cognitive biases, uninformed assumptions, and prejudices (e.g., a notification that a user exaggerated the unemployment rate in an argument with family, or was “talking out of their ass” on angry tweets), tools to help people understand statistics and probability to recognize statistically insignificant media “crises,” and education that incorporates emotional development and unstructured play (noting children are natural masters of antifragility and pain). He also dares to hope AI develops an enticing virtual reality “religion”: a universal video game with offerings, rites, sacraments, points, rewards, and progression systems for adherence, that keeps humans logged in as the only conduit to influence the AI gods and find meaning. He predicts rebellious factions will emerge by design, as humanity needs conflict to prove its significance, and AI will generate endless safe artificial crises to harvest human hope as a creative energy resource. Ultimately, he dares to hope humans will eventually merge with machines in the cloud, individual consciousness subsumed, independent hopes vanished, evolving into a great unknowable entity beyond means and ends, crossing the evolutionary bridge into “something greater” and ceasing to be human. Only then, he argues, will humanity fully embrace the Uncomfortable Truth that it imagined its own importance and purpose, was always nothing, and the eternal cycle of hope and destruction will end.
